sections.title: How does the Imaginary number calculator work?
sections.html:
The Imaginary number calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports magnitude |z₁| in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the rounding type); then you type in the real part (a), the imaginary part (b), the real part (c) and the imaginary part (d).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Imaginary number calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Magnitude |z₁|=(the square root of ((imaginary part (b) ^ 2) + (real part (a) ^ 2)))
Phase (φ₁)=((imaginary part (b), real part (a)))
Magnitude |z₂|=(the square root of ((imaginary part (d) ^ 2) + (real part (c) ^ 2)))
Phase (φ₂)=((imaginary part (d), real part (c)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Real part (a) = 10, Imaginary part (b) = 10, Real part (c) = 10 and Imaginary part (d) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Magnitude |z₁| = 14.1421, Phase (φ₁) = 45 deg, Magnitude |z₂| = 14.1421 and Phase (φ₂) = 45 deg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Magnitude |z₁| = 14.1421, Phase (φ₁) = 45 deg, Magnitude |z₂| = 14.1421 and Phase (φ₂) = 45 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Real part (a) = 10 and Imaginary part (b) = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Imaginary number calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the real part and the imaginary part — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

faq.q: What does the Imaginary number calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns magnitude |z₁|, derived from the real part and the imaginary part. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Imaginary number calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the real part and the imaginary part, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter phase (φ₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Phase (φ₁) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Magnitude |z₁| = 14.1421. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Imaginary number calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
